rv.q: Ultimately, they scrape together a delicious, delirious portrait of this largely unknown juggernaut.
But even as it works to cast Lempicka in a new light, this complex artist still remains just beyond the frame.
Too often history gets the airbrush here, inviting the same criticism that Marinetti lobbed at Lempicka: decorative.

The result is a breathless, up-tempo force march through some of the darkest decades in European history, and a big, messy, fascinating life is processed into a theater piece that is just big and messy.
“Lempicka” often seems to be all visible brushstrokes, a neatly constructed but surprisingly conventional show that turns the wild, imperious and wayward woman into a fairly standard-issue heroine.
Lempicka the woman was unquestionably fascinating, flawed, and fabulous; Lempicka the musical often goes flat.
Shoving de Lempicka so aggressively through today’s ideological and aesthetic filters, unconscious as the act may be, has the effect of nullifying her singular ambivalence and complexity.
They have what the musical lacks: a clear and compelling aesthetic.
And so, the ugly splatter that audiences are left to parse is a ridiculous two-and-half-hour Eurovision act with stratospheric delusions of grandeur.
Commanding, towering songs that take your breath and demand your attention and a story that is staggering and sexy.
Ultimately, Lempicka is ravishing — and one of the best new musicals this season.
Lempicka is an undeniably compelling and original piece of art, unique within a season dominated by musicals based on existing films or musical catalogs.

It’s Tamara’s mission to capture that life, and if “Lempicka” doesn’t match its subject’s glowing virtuosity — or that of better musicals, for that matter — it should at least inspire more interest in her work.
It’s too bad the result ends up being more artsy-fartsy than dramatically or musically compelling.
But the songs and scenes ultimately add up to an almost mechanical-feeling sameness, loud and overwhelming.
Lempicka looks good, it could’ve been good, it could still be good given some more polish and judicious editing, but in its current state, it’s just a poor imitation of a good musical.
In other words, Kreitzer, Gould and director Chavkin rely on the cast to turn second-rate material into first-rate audience-grabbers.
Messy and maddening, new musical Lempicka has all the pedigree for something groundbreaking but never finds its own distinctive form.
Turns out, the fascinating life of the undervalued painter that inspired them proves a slippery subject to sustain in this occasionally arresting but overstuffed and tonally jumbled show.
In the end, “Lempicka” takes a potentially fascinating character and turns her into another weepy, boring victim.

But she cannot overcome the fact that she is working with a cliché-ridden show about an artist who is undoubtedly interesting but who is painted only in slashes and slathers of color that prevent us from seeing her as an actual human being.
Personally, I’d rather just brush the whole experience off.
Lempicka deserves – deserved – better.
Unfortunately, neither the score nor the book lives up to her high standards.

Herein lies Lempicka’s challenge: the musical wants to capitalize on Madonna and other pop stars’ notoriety along with sense of agency uncommon to female artists of the era, but its creators have stretched the canvas so thin that the brush strokes crack.
But there’s no disguising that this is a messy show with a talented but ultimately too enigmatic character at its center.
It was hard to listen and engage when the music was, quite literally, painful to my ears.
If only the sexualization of women and their nudity in art were not so standard.
The current book just slides from one scene in Lempicka's life to the next, without taking time to develop her character or those of the people around her.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this visually striking musical about painter Tamara de Lempicka, praising Eden Espinosa's performance and bold design but faulting a muddled, overstuffed narrative that struggles to find its artistic focus.

vs.sum: The Longacre Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, even from the balcony, and the sound quality is consistently praised. While the seating is a bit narrow, it provides average comfort for most patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant Beaux Arts interior, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue, with some lines at intermission but generally manageable.

acc.note: Small restroom-only elevator (may not accommodate all wheelchairs). 3 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra.

vr.q: I think any show that has such a clear vision has the potential to be quite polarizing so I don't know if the show will appeal to everyone but I was into it and the production is undeniably impressive.
I think it's a very great production of just an okay musical, but I also think it's very fixable over preview.
I wanted to love it more than I did... I didn't hate it. It's something that I would probably see again if I was able to get a discount ticket, but it. I just. I wanted to love it.
